Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployments
Latency and throughput tradeoffs for clinical pipelines
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — super excited. Quick audio check?
[00:12] Dr. Lena Park (Blue River): Sounds good on our end, can hear you.
[00:18] Rajiv (Blue River): Yep, loud and clear.
[00:22] Maya: Awesome. So we're recording this as a short customer spotlight — we'll keep it informal, aim for 15–20 minutes of on-the-record conversation and the rest can be off the record if need be.
[00:35] Omar (Redwood PMM): Just to add, we'll share a draft edit and two social blurbs after — nothing published without your sign-off.
[00:42] Sofia (Blue River): Perfect.
[00:45] Maya: Great, okay Dr. Park, can you kick us off — tell listeners briefly what Blue River does and where the inference piece fits?
[00:55] Dr. Lena Park: Sure — Blue River is a clinical diagnostics platform, we run high-throughput blood panel analysis and use ML to identify anomalous markers. The inference piece is… is in the clinical report generation and triage stage. So models summarize lab outputs into a clinician-friendly narrative, highlight flags, suggest next steps. Saves our lab techs a lot of time.
[01:22] Tess (Redwood SE): Quick clarifying Q — are those models hosted on-prem currently? I know you mentioned a hybrid earlier.
[01:29] Rajiv: Yeah we have an internal cluster for PHI processing but a lot of the NLP summarization used to be on prem and was… sort of brittle. We moved to Redwood to get consistent latency and ops.
[01:40] Maya: Nice, can you describe the migration? Was it an incremental pilot or a big flip?
[01:46] Rajiv: Incremental — we started with a non-PHI sandbox where we sent anonymized results to Redwood's hosted API. The initial thing we cared about was throughput, we had like bursts during morning shift where hundreds of reports needed quick summaries.
[02:04] Dr. Lena Park: And accuracy; the quality of the model outputs was actually better once we used Redwood's model catalog with the tuned variants. I know the team there helped us pick a smaller quantized model that still preserved the clinical phrasing.
[02:19] Omar: That's a great point — we often recommend quantization profiles for cost without losing medical terminology. We call it— I always forget — the runtime will do kernel selection and a quant profile.
[02:31] Maya: (laughs) The black box of kernels. Tess: We have a cheat-sheet that maps model families to kernel characteristics — we'll send that after.
[02:41] Sofia: We also liked Redwood's caching — the prefix/KV cache meant repeated patient phrasing didn't re-cost tokens every time, which was a big cost win for us.
[02:53] Dr. Lena Park: There was this one weekend where a vendor drop created a spike, and the cache smoothed it out — saved us from throttling.
[03:03] Maya: Nice, and on the security side — Rajiv, you mentioned concerns early on about PHI. Can you walk listeners through your controls and how Redwood fitted?
[03:13] Rajiv: Sure. For PHI we couldn't use the hosted public API for the production set — we used Redwood Private deployed into our VPC. That gave us customer-managed KMS, strict egress rules, and audit logs. Redwood's audit logs were helpful during our internal review — although the label in the logs read 'Redwood Privet' in our early notes, so that was a cute typo in the first run.
[03:36] Tess: (laughs) I — I remember that.
[03:40] Dr. Lena Park: The SOC2 doc was the key. Once we had the compliance deck and the KMS mapping, our security council signed off.
[03:48] Omar: We usually share the SOC2 summary and a one-pager for architectural controls — bit.ly/redwood-sec-sum is the one we use internally.
[03:58] Maya: Switching to performance — what numbers did you see after moving the summarizer to Redwood Dedicated?
[04:05] Rajiv: For our 512-token typical job the p95 latency dropped from ~1.2s on-prem to 380ms on Dedicated in us-east. Throughput increased too — we could serve peak batches without manual autoscale tweaks.
[04:20] Dr. Lena Park: Practically that meant our lab techs had results surfaced in their dashboard in under a minute instead of waiting for a batch to finish at end of shift.
[04:29] Maya: Were there cost surprises? Any trade-offs?
[04:32] Rajiv: Initially people expected the cloud to be cheaper but the cost per token was higher. The win was overall staff time saved. Then Redwood Optimize suggested batching plus a quantized mid-size model and running prefix caching — it reduced unit cost by maybe 35–40%. That made the math obvious.
[04:53] Sofia: And we used the usage analytics to show finance the ROI story. The token breakdown per workflow was super helpful.
[05:02] Omar: Can I ask about model rollouts — how do you handle canaries in a regulated environment?
[05:08] Dr. Lena Park: We do a multi-tier rollout: first sandbox with synthetic data, then a shadow run on 5% of live traffic with logging only, then a canary for a single clinic partner. Redwood's canary feature plus automatic fallback to the previous variant helped. There was one time we had a phrasing regression and the auto-fallback triggered which was a lifesaver.
[05:32] Tess: We also instrument quality monitors tied to prompt sets; if redwood-diff detects a regression we alert the ML team. Sometimes the transcriber misheard 'redwood-diff' as 'red wood diff' in the logs, but it's the same tool.
[05:45] Rajiv: (chuckles) We'll need to clean up some of our internal docs.
[05:49] Maya: Switching gears to the marketing side — what made you want to participate in a customer story?
[05:55] Dr. Lena Park: We get a lot of inbound from hospitals asking about both reliability and regulatory posture. Showing a concrete clinical workflow and numbers helps prospective partners understand the fit. Also, there was enthusiasm among the engineering team to highlight the operational wins.
[06:10] Sofia: And it's great PR for clinical recruiting — we get candidates who cite these kinds of case studies.
[06:15] Maya: Wonderful. We'll capture a short quote from Dr. Park for the header. Do you have one in mind now or would you prefer to draft and send?
[06:23] Dr. Lena Park: I'll draft one — maybe 2 sentences: something about reduction in turnaround time and confidence in audits. I'll send it to Maya.
[06:30] Omar: We'll also send a draft episode outline and two social posts — nothing goes out until you approve.
[06:36] Maya: Quick audio note — Rajiv, you had a bit of echo in the first four minutes; we'll edit that out of the published cut.
[06:44] Rajiv: Yep, thanks.
[06:46] Maya: Any closing technical tips for teams trying to run similar workflows?
[06:50] Rajiv: Start with a sandbox and synthetic PHI, automate canaries and shadow runs, invest in prefix caching early — it pays off. Also, set clear success metrics: latency p95 under target, and a clinical accuracy check-list for the outputs.
[07:08] Dr. Lena Park: And involve your compliance folks early. They can guide you on what audit trails you'll need.
[07:13] Tess: Totally. From the Redwood side, we'll include our audit-log mapping doc and a KMS integration checklist in the follow-up.
[07:21] Maya: Great. We'll pause the formal recording now and go into a short off-the-record chat about potential customer referrals and a quote wording. Thanks everyone for being candid — this will make a great short customer piece.
[07:33] Sofia: Thanks, and thanks for the edit review window.
[07:36] Maya: Thanks all.
[07:38] [off-record chatter starts — not transcribed]
[47:55] [file end]
